A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same partner-modelling study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Overcooked experiments measuring collaborative performance, hidden-state representations, adaptation to changing partners and blind-agent performance.

after.justification: v2 retains the original Overcooked results and adds original CoinGame experiments and representation analyses in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The PPO-trained GRU agent and task-allocation mechanism are retained. Appendix B.2 newly documents the CNN, fully connected layers and actor/critic heads, without establishing an architecture modification. CoinGame applies the existing framework to another environment.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only Overcooked-AI, including five layouts, partner switching and blind observations. v2 adds training and evaluation in modified CoinGame, where agents divide red/blue coin collection according to partners' action-success probabilities. This substantially extends task coverage beyond cooking.

E2.justification: The existing Overcooked comparisons retain the MLP, single-partner RNN and no-influence RNN variants, with the random-input probe control where applicable. CoinGame reuses these agent variants. Newly discussed attention and explicit-modelling approaches are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A introduces a CoinGame protocol with 10 million training timesteps, four training and five evaluation skill profiles, and coin-count and correct-colour allocation metrics. Separately, Section 5.2 now describes probe testing on held-out partners, although Appendix B.3.3 retains the original 80/20 rollout-seed split; an actual change to that split is unresolved.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a focused analysis of which individual hidden units track partner skill, using correlations and mean-activation heatmaps over 1,000 evaluation episodes. This extends the existing population-level UMAP and probing analyses. The original Overcooked controls remain, with analogous representation analyses also reported for CoinGame.

E5.justification: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals already appear in v1. v2 additionally reports CoinGame performance uncertainty across five random training seeds in Figure 5, whereas the retained Overcooked procedure selects the best of five training seeds. No increase in runs for the existing experiments is documented.

E6.justification: Figures 5–7 add substantial CoinGame results: the multi-partner RNN leads the performance and probing comparisons, and Appendix A reports 16 of 32 hidden units with absolute skill correlation of at least 0.5. The existing Overcooked results are retained, including blind-agent scores of 9.43, 5.8 and 1.08 soups per episode for the multi-partner RNN, single-partner RNN and MLP.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, recurrent-state update and expected-return objective are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. CoinGame's skill and reward notation describes the additional experiment rather than introducing a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and central discussion claims remain: generic recurrent agents develop partner representations without dedicated modelling objectives, generalise to unfamiliar partners and depend on suitable collaborative pressure. CoinGame adds support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges the MLP's fivebyfive advantage already visible in Figure 2 and proposes simpler coordination requirements as an explanation. It explains incomplete post-switch recovery through subtask asymmetry, and adds qualifications concerning direct control of partners, scaling to multiple teammates and possible modelling shortcuts. These refine the existing interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds architecture, normalization and observation-preprocessing details; Section 4.3.1 clarifies that training and evaluation partner pairs are disjoint. CoinGame's training budget and partner sampling are documented. Existing hyperparameter tables and code access remain, but the direct video link is replaced by a general reference to supplementary materials.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2–2.5 substantially broaden research positioning through social influence, zero-shot coordination, recurrent meta-learning, cognitive and economic prediction theories, and attention architectures. Added discussions connect the findings to work by Jaques, Wang, Clark and Harsanyi, among others, rather than merely adding incidental citations.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain. v2 adds related-work subsections, targeted methodological explanations and discussion paragraphs, and reorganizes the appendix into CoinGame results and additional details. Editorial defects include an unresolved citation in Section 2.4 and a stray question-mark placeholder in Section 4.3.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material in Figures 5–7: the CoinGame environment and performance comparisons, representation/probing plots, and hidden-unit correlation and activation displays. Figure 1 is resized and redrawn with different speed illustrations. Existing Overcooked plots and tables are retained; the layout illustration moves from Figure 5 to Figure 8.

improvement.justification: The preliminary CoinGame replication broadens support beyond v1's single environment, while architecture disclosures and more explicit qualifications improve transparency. These gains are limited by incomplete integration: v2's held-out-partner probe description conflicts with its retained seed-split procedure, and the discussion still incorrectly states that only one environment was studied. The added evidence supports a modest net improvement despite these reporting defects.
